**The circuit.** The \(8\ \Omega\) and the \(6\ \Omega\) resistors lie one behind the other in the single upper branch of the loop, and the \(5\ \mathrm{V}\) cell sits in the lower branch. There is only one conducting path, so the same current must pass through both resistors: they are in **series**. This is the arrangement of Fig. 11.9.

**a] Potential difference across the \(8\ \Omega\) resistor**

In a series combination the supply voltage is divided between the resistors while the current remains the same in all of them, and the equivalent resistance is the sum of the individual resistances:

\(R_s = R_1 + R_2 = 8 + 6 = 14\ \Omega\)

The current drawn from the supply is therefore

\(I = \dfrac{V}{R_s} = \dfrac{5}{14} = 0.357\ \mathrm{A}\)

This same current passes through the \(8\ \Omega\) resistor, so by Ohm's law the potential difference across it is

\(V_1 = I R_1 = \dfrac{5}{14} \times 8 = \dfrac{20}{7} = 2.86\ \mathrm{V}\)

**Check.** The \(6\ \Omega\) resistor then carries \(V_2 = \dfrac{5}{14} \times 6 = \dfrac{15}{7} = 2.14\ \mathrm{V}\), and \(V_1 + V_2 = 2.86 + 2.14 = 5\ \mathrm{V}\), the whole supply voltage — which is what a series combination requires.

**b] The potential difference across the \(8\ \Omega\) resistor becomes LARGER.**

Let the third resistor be \(R\), joined in parallel with the \(6\ \Omega\) resistor. For a parallel combination the reciprocal of the equivalent resistance is the sum of the reciprocals of the individual resistances:

\(\dfrac{1}{R_p} = \dfrac{1}{6} + \dfrac{1}{R} \qquad \therefore\ R_p = \dfrac{6R}{6+R}\)

Since \(\dfrac{1}{R}\) is positive for any real resistor, \(\dfrac{1}{R_p} > \dfrac{1}{6}\), and hence \(R_p < 6\ \Omega\). **Giving the current an extra path can only lower the resistance of that part of the circuit; it can never raise it.**

The \(8\ \Omega\) resistor is untouched and is still in series with this section, so the total resistance of the circuit falls below \(14\ \Omega\) and the current supplied by the cell,

\(I = \dfrac{5}{8 + R_p}\)

increases. A larger current through an unchanged \(8\ \Omega\) resistor means a larger potential difference across it:

\(V_1 = I \times 8 = \dfrac{5 \times 8}{8 + R_p}\)

With \(R_p < 6\ \Omega\) the denominator is smaller than the \(8 + 6 = 14\) it was before, so \(V_1\) is greater than \(\dfrac{20}{7} = 2.86\ \mathrm{V}\).

**Illustration.** If the third resistor were \(R = 12\ \Omega\), then \(R_p = \dfrac{6 \times 12}{6 + 12} = 4\ \Omega\), the total resistance would be \(8 + 4 = 12\ \Omega\), the current would be \(I = \dfrac{5}{12} = 0.417\ \mathrm{A}\), and the potential difference across the \(8\ \Omega\) resistor would be \(0.417 \times 8 = 3.33\ \mathrm{V}\) — larger than the original \(2.86\ \mathrm{V}\).

**In short.** The two sections act as a potential divider across the fixed \(5\ \mathrm{V}\) supply. Adding a resistor in parallel with the \(6\ \Omega\) reduces that section's resistance and so reduces its share of the supply voltage, which leaves a bigger share for the \(8\ \Omega\) resistor.

**To prove:** the current density \(J\) of a metallic conductor is directly proportional to the drift speed \(V_d\) of its free electrons.

**Set-up.** Consider a metallic conductor of uniform cross-sectional area \(A\), and look at a length \(L\) of it. Let \(n\) be the number of free electrons per unit volume of the wire and \(e\) the magnitude of the charge on an electron. It is assumed that all the electrons move with the same drift speed \(V_d\), and that the current \(I\) is the same throughout the cross section \(A\).

**Step 1 — the free charge contained in the length \(L\).** That length has volume \(AL\), so it contains \(nAL\) free electrons, and the total charge carried by them is

\(q = nALe\)

**Step 2 — the time in which that charge crosses a section.** The electrons drift with speed \(V_d\), so an electron takes

\(t = \dfrac{L}{V_d}\)

to travel the length \(L\). In this time the whole of the charge \(q\) passes through a given cross section of the wire.

**Step 3 — the current.** By the definition of current, \(I = \dfrac{q}{t}\). Substituting the two results above,

\(I = \dfrac{nALe}{L/V_d} = nAV_de\)

**Step 4 — the current density.** Current density is the current per unit area of cross section, \(J = \dfrac{I}{A}\). Therefore

\(J = \dfrac{nAV_de}{A} = neV_d\)

that is, \(J = (ne)V_d\).

**Conclusion.** For a given metallic conductor, \(n\) is the number of free electrons per unit volume — a fixed property of that metal — and \(e\) is a universal constant, so the factor \(ne\) is a constant. Hence

\(J \propto V_d\)

The current density is directly proportional to the drift speed of the electrons, the constant of proportionality being \(ne\). The SI unit of \(J\) is \(\mathrm{A}/\mathrm{m}^2\).

**A note on direction.** Written as vectors the result reads \(\vec{J} = (ne)\vec{V}_d\). For electrons the quantity \(ne\) is negative, so \(\vec{J}\) and \(\vec{V}_d\) point in opposite directions — the conventional current is directed opposite to the drift of the electrons. This does not affect the proportionality between their magnitudes, which is what has been proved.

Ohm's law states that the current \(I\) through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference \(V\) applied across its two ends, provided the physical state of the conductor is unchanged. Substances are classified by whether or not they obey it.

| Point of difference | Ohmic (linear) substances | Non-ohmic (non-linear) substances |
|---|---|---|
| Ohm's law | Obeyed: \(I \propto V\), so \(V = IR\) | Not obeyed: \(I\) is not proportional to \(V\) |
| \(I\)-\(V\) characteristic | A straight line passing through the origin (Fig. 11.4) | Not a straight line; it is a curve (Fig. 11.5) |
| Resistance | Constant — \(V/I\) has the same value at every point of the characteristic | Not constant — it is a function of \(V\) or of \(I\) |
| How the resistance is obtained | \(R = \dfrac{V}{I}\), a single number valid over the whole range | \(R = \dfrac{dV}{dI}\), the slope at one particular operating point |
| Examples | Metallic conductors, e.g. a copper wire or a nichrome wire | Liquid electrolytes, vacuum tubes, junction diodes, thermistors |

For a non-ohmic device the resistance at a particular value of the potential difference \(V\) has to be defined as a limit,

\(R = \displaystyle\lim_{\Delta I \to 0} \dfrac{\Delta V}{\Delta I} = \dfrac{dV}{dI}\)

where \(\Delta V\) is the potential difference between the two values \(V - \dfrac{\Delta V}{2}\) and \(V + \dfrac{\Delta V}{2}\), and \(\Delta I\) is the corresponding change in the current.

**Explanation with examples.**

*An ohmic substance — a metal wire.* Keep a copper wire at a constant temperature and apply increasing potential differences across it. If \(1\ \mathrm{V}\) drives a current of \(0.5\ \mathrm{A}\), then \(2\ \mathrm{V}\) drives \(1\ \mathrm{A}\) and \(3\ \mathrm{V}\) drives \(1.5\ \mathrm{A}\). The ratio \(\dfrac{V}{I}\) works out to \(2\ \Omega\) every single time, so one number, \(R = 2\ \Omega\), describes the wire completely, and the graph of \(I\) against \(V\) is a straight line through the origin.

*A non-ohmic substance — a junction diode.* Below a certain threshold voltage the diode passes almost no current; beyond it the current rises very steeply. The ratio \(\dfrac{V}{I}\) is therefore enormous at a low voltage and small at a higher one, so no single value of \(R\) can describe the diode. Its resistance must be quoted for the particular voltage at which it is working, as the slope \(\dfrac{dV}{dI}\) of its characteristic there.

**The condition matters.** Ohm's law holds only "provided the physical state of the conductor is unchanged". A metal wire behaves ohmically only while its temperature is held constant; if the current heats it, its resistivity changes and its \(I\)-\(V\) graph bends away from a straight line.

**Only the current remains constant along the conductor.** Both the current density and the drift speed change from place to place.

**Why the current is the same at every cross section.** The current is a steady direct current, so nothing in the conductor changes with time and charge does not pile up anywhere inside the metal. Whatever charge crosses one section in a given time must therefore cross every other section in that same time — if a wide part passed more charge per second than a narrow part, charge would accumulate between them and the current would not be steady. Put another way, successive slices of the piece lie one behind the other along a single electrical path, that is, in series, and the same current flows through every element of a series combination. Hence \(I\) is the same everywhere.

**Why the current density is not constant.** Current density is the current per unit area of cross section:

\(J = \dfrac{I}{A}\)

Here \(I\) is fixed, but \(A\) differs from place to place because the cross-section is non-uniform. Therefore

\(J \propto \dfrac{1}{A}\)

so \(J\) is largest where the piece is thinnest and smallest where it is thickest.

**Why the drift speed is not constant either.** From \(I = nAV_de\),

\(V_d = \dfrac{I}{nAe} = \dfrac{J}{ne}\)

The free-electron density \(n\) and the electronic charge \(e\) are properties of the metal and are the same throughout one piece of it, and \(I\) has just been shown to be constant. Hence

\(V_d \propto \dfrac{1}{A}\)

The electrons drift faster through the narrow parts of the piece and more slowly through the wide parts — in the same way that water flowing through a pipe speeds up where the pipe narrows. Since \(J = neV_d\), the current density and the drift speed rise and fall together, and neither of them is constant.

**Answer:** of the three quantities named, only the **current** remains constant along the conductor.
